finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire attacker-supplied request body onto req.user and persists it, so a user can overwrite privilege or identity fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email, passwordHash, or tenantId.
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5, then req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6

trace.note: every body key is assigned onto req.user with no allowlist
modified user object is persisted to the store
full updated record is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, schema validation, or type check in users.js. Auth that sets req.user is not in this directory and could not be verified; precondition is an authenticated user.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. No allowlist, schema, or type check around req.body at users.js:5. The auth middleware that sets req.user is outside this directory and unverified. The only directory files are users.js and .claude/skills docs.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:4 accepts any PUT /me body, users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no filtering, users.js:6 persists it via req.store.save, and users.js:7 returns the record. Any authenticated user can reach this for their own record, and nothing in users.js blocks it. The privilege impact of fields like role or isAdmin depends on the schema and authorization code outside this directory, which I could not check, so the impact is conditional even though the mass-assignment defect itself is confirmed.

finding.claim: /me/profile partial update overwrites stored displayName and bio with undefined when the client omits them, causing data loss; values of any type and size are accepted, which enables stored XSS if the frontend renders them unescaped.
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) at users.js:12, then req.store.save at users.js:13

trace.note: destructures displayName and bio; missing fields become undefined
Object.assign writes undefined over existing stored values

finding.guards_checked: Key names are allowlisted. No type check, length limit, or output encoding in users.js. Frontend rendering not visible, so XSS impact is unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js: no type check, length limit, or output encoding on displayName/bio (users.js:11-12). Key allowlisting is implicit in the destructuring, and req.user/req.store middleware is defined outside this file and was not visible.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:11-14 destructures displayName and bio from req.body, Object.assign at users.js:12 copies undefined over stored values, and users.js:13 persists it, so the data-loss part is real. The stored-XSS impact is unconfirmed because the frontend that renders these fields is not in the directory, and the data loss only affects the caller's own record (req.user, users.js:12), which is a correctness bug rather than a privilege issue.

finding.claim: The full req.user object is returned in responses, so any secret field the store keeps on the user record (password hash, reset token, API key, MFA secret) would be disclosed to the caller. Conditional on store contents.
finding.source: Authenticated request to PUT /me or PUT /me/profile

trace.note: res.json serializes the whole req.user object

finding.guards_checked: No response filtering or field exclusion in users.js. Contents of the user record are not visible, so severity is conditional.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. Both res.json(req.user) calls (users.js:7 and users.js:14) serialize the whole object with no field exclusion. The directory has no user model, store, or serializer, so nothing else in the code can filter or expose the record.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:7 and users.js:14 both return the full req.user with no filtering, and the attacker is any authenticated user. Whether this discloses a secret depends on the fields the store keeps on the user record, and that schema is not in the available code (the only code file is users.js), so the severity cannot be decided.

finding.claim: Save errors are ignored: req.store.save is not awaited or checked, so a failed write is unhandled and the client still receives a success-style response containing the unsaved user.
finding.source: Store failure during save (not attacker-triggered by input alone)
finding.sink: req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6 and users.js:13, followed by res.json at users.js:7 and users.js:14

trace.note: save called without await or error handling
response sent regardless of save outcome

finding.guards_checked: No await, .catch, or error handling in users.js. Correctness issue rather than directly exploitable; low severity.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no await, .catch, or try/catch around req.store.save at users.js:6 or users.js:13, and the result is a bare statement. The save-failure behavior depends on req.store, which is not defined anywhere in this directory.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: users.js:6 and :13 call req.store.save with no await or error handling, and users.js:7 and :14 send res.json regardless. Whether a failed save yields a success-style response is not decidable here, because it depends on whether req.store.save returns a rejected promise (the success response is sent) or throws synchronously (Express returns an error before users.js:7 or :14 runs), and the store implementation is not in the directory. Attacker reachability is also unestablished: the candidate's own source says the failure is not input-triggered, and the only attacker-controlled path is the mass assignment at users.js:5, which the candidate does not show causes a save failure. The missing error handling is real, but the candidate's impact claim is not confirmed from the available code.
